narrative_story:
# The Thirty-Seven Letters of Monk Hideo, As Compiled by His Opponent

---

## Editor's Preface

In the autumn tournament of 1951, held at the Butokuden in Kyoto during the first full season in which the Allied occupation authorities permitted formal competition with live blades, Hideo Takeshi won eleven consecutive bouts in three days. This is a matter of public record. I was his opponent in the twelfth.

The circumstances of that final match have been described elsewhere, often inaccurately. I will state only what can be verified: that Hideo entered with the highest score of the tournament; that I entered with the second highest; that the bout lasted less than four seconds; that Hideo, having drawn and initiated his cut, arrested the blade and stepped back; that he laid his sword on the floor of the hall; that he bowed—not to me, not to the judges, but in the direction of the tokonoma alcove, which held a single branch of autumn maple—and left the building. He did not speak. The judges recorded a forfeit. I was awarded the tournament. I have held the title for forty-one years, and there is not a morning I have carried it without weight.

Hideo's disappearance from competitive swordsmanship was discussed extensively in the months that followed. I will not rehearse the speculation. I took no part in it. I resumed my training. I taught. I grew older.

Fourteen months after the forfeit, in December of 1952, I received a letter. It had been posted from Fukui Prefecture. The paper was coarse, handmade, flecked with fragments of bark that I later identified as *mitsumata*—a paper stock associated with the mountain monasteries of that region. The letter bore no return address. Hideo's hand was immediately recognizable: the severe vertical strokes, the refusal of cursive abbreviation, the ink ground so heavily the characters sat raised on the page like small scars.

The letter contained no greeting, no inquiry after my health, no acknowledgment that anything had passed between us. It consisted of four paragraphs discussing a phrase from Miyamoto Musashi's *Gorin no Sho*—specifically, the passage in the Water Book in which Musashi describes *ma-ai*, the correct distance between opponents. Hideo's argument, developed with a precision I will call excessive, was that the standard reading of *ma-ai* as spatial interval failed to account for Musashi's use of the character *ai*, which carries connotations of meeting, of mutual arrival, and which appears elsewhere in compounds related to moral fitness and reciprocal obligation. He proposed that Musashi was describing not the distance at which a sword can reach flesh but the distance at which two minds can reach each other's intention—that *ma-ai* was, properly understood, an ethical rather than geometric concept, and that a swordsman who maintained correct distance was not protecting his body but honoring his opponent's right to be fully perceived.

I read the letter twice. I nearly discarded it. I placed it in the drawer of my writing desk beneath a sheaf of tournament records, where it remained for three weeks before I read it again and understood it was the first sentence of a conversation I had not agreed to enter.

Over the next thirty-nine years, thirty-six additional letters arrived. Their frequency was irregular—sometimes three in a single season, sometimes silences of two or three years during which I did not know whether Hideo was alive. The paper changed as the decades passed, growing thinner and more refined, as though he were learning the craft himself or finding a better source. The brushwork changed as well: the early letters are dense and controlled, the characters pressed into the page with a force that occasionally tore the fibers; the later letters are spare, the brush barely touching, as though he were trying to write with the shadow of his hand rather than the hand itself.

I answered none of them.

I present the letters here in the order I received them, which I believe to be the order in which they were written, though I cannot be certain. Each letter is followed by my annotations, which I have limited to points of clarification: identifications of the texts Hideo references, corrections of occasional errors in his citations, and, where necessary, brief contextual remarks to assist the reader unfamiliar with the traditions under discussion.

Several of the letters contain ink-wash drawings—small studies of natural subjects, never labeled—which I have reproduced where the printing process permits. In cases where the paper has been damaged by water or age, I have indicated illegible passages with brackets. Letters Fourteen and Fifteen arrived in a single envelope and may have been composed on the same occasion; I have separated them for readability but note their shared postmark. Letter Twenty-Two was written on the reverse of what appears to be a page from a monastic account book, columns of figures for rice and lamp oil faintly visible beneath the characters. I have not attempted to translate the accounts.

One final note on method. In several letters, Hideo's brush leaves the page mid-character, producing marks that may be incomplete words, deliberate gestures, or the traces of interrupted thought. I have reproduced these as faithfully as I can, consulting when necessary with specialists in Hideo's calligraphic lineage, though the results have not always been conclusive. The reader will encounter these ambiguities and must make of them what the reader can. I have tried not to resolve what Hideo did not resolve. Whether I have succeeded in this is not for me to say.

—Arakawa Noboru
Kyoto, March 1992

---

## The Letters

---

### Letter One

*Received December 1952. Postmarked Fukui Prefecture. Paper: heavy kozo stock, hand-pressed, with visible bark inclusions. Ink: sumi, very dark, ground to an unusual density.*

---

You will know the passage.

In the Water Book, Musashi writes that the swordsman must understand *ma-ai* before he can understand anything else—that all technique proceeds from correct distance, and that a man who cannot perceive the interval between himself and his opponent has not yet begun to practice the art.

This is read, universally, as instruction in measurement. The commentators describe it in terms of sword-lengths, of the precise reach of the extended arm, of the half-step that brings the blade from the edge of contact into the killing line. Yamada draws diagrams. Ochiai provides tables. Even Arima, who is otherwise perceptive, reduces the passage to a problem of geometry—as though Musashi, who killed sixty men and then retired to a cave to paint birds, had nothing more to communicate than the optimal distance for a downward cut.

I propose that they have misread the character.

*Ai* does not only mean interval. It appears in *ai-te*, the opponent, the one who meets you. It appears in *ai-uchi*, the simultaneous strike, the mutual kill. It appears in *ainaka*, the space between—but the *between* of a relationship, not of a measurement. The *between* that describes what lies in the space connecting two people who are aware of each other.

If Musashi meant only reach, he could have written *kyori*. He did not. He chose a word that contains the opponent inside it.

The correct distance, then, is not the distance at which I can strike you. It is the distance at which I can *know* you—at which your intention becomes legible to me and mine to you, at which we are no longer two separate figures performing separate calculations but a single system whose movements are mutually determined. To maintain correct distance is to sustain the act of perception. To close distance is to end it—to choose the cut over the seeing, the result over the relationship.

This is what the commentators do not say, because to say it would require them to admit that Musashi's *ma-ai* renders every completed duel a failure of understanding. That the strike, however perfect, is the moment the swordsman stops perceiving his opponent and begins merely destroying him.

I have been thinking about this for fourteen months. I find that I am not yet done.

An ink-wash study of two pine branches, nearly touching, accompanies the letter's final page.

---

**Editor's annotation:** The passage Hideo references is from Chapter 2 of the *Gorin no Sho* (1645). His characterization of the standard commentaries is accurate, if uncharitable. Yamada Jirokichi's diagrams appear in *Gorin no Sho Kaisetsu* (1922); Ochiai Torahei's measurements in *Kenpo no Kokoro* (1937); Arima Kōshū's discussion in *Musashi to Sono Jidai* (1941). The reading of *ai* that Hideo proposes is linguistically defensible, though I am aware of no prior commentator who has advanced it.

---

### Letter Two

*Received February 1953. Postmarked Fukui Prefecture. Paper: same stock as Letter One, though lighter in weight. Ink: somewhat less dense; prepared, perhaps, with more water.*

---

Musashi did not duel after the age of thirty. This is well known. What is not sufficiently remarked upon is the manner of his final encounter—the fight with Sasaki Kojirō on the island of Ganryū, in which Musashi arrived late, fought with a wooden sword carved from an oar, struck Kojirō dead, and then immediately retreated by boat before the fallen man's students could reach him.

The commentators treat the lateness as gamesmanship, the wooden sword as bravado, the retreat as pragmatism. In no account I have read does anyone ask the simplest question: Why did he stop?

A man who wins sixty duels does not stop because he has run out of opponents. He stops because something in the sixty-first possibility has become intolerable. What changes between the sixtieth fight and the refusal of the sixty-first?

I think he saw something in Kojirō's guard. I think he saw it before the fight began—on the beach, in the moment of approach, when both men's stances declared themselves across that distance I wrote to you about—and I think what he saw was not an opportunity but a *condition*. An exposure so fundamental it could not be exploited without committing an act closer to surgery than combat. And I think the wooden sword was his compromise: to win without the irreversible consequence of having cut through what he had perceived, to leave the knowledge unexpressed in steel.

That he killed Kojirō anyway was, I believe, the source of his retirement. He had tried to find a way to see without destroying, and he had failed. The wooden sword killed as efficiently as any blade. Perception, once achieved, could not be made harmless.

This may be wrong. I have had only the winter to consider it, and winters here are long but not infinite.

*A drawing of a boat seen from above, as though by a bird. The water around it is rendered in a single wash. There is no figure in the boat.*

---

**Editor's annotation:** The duel between Musashi and Sasaki Kojirō took place on April 13, 1612, on Ganryū Island in the Kanmon Straits. Hideo's account of the details—the lateness, the oar, the retreat—is consistent with the standard sources, principally the *Niten Ki* (c. 1776). His interpretation of Musashi's retirement is, so far as I know, entirely his own.

I note that the final sentence—"winters here are long but not infinite"—is the closest Hideo comes in the early letters to acknowledging his physical circumstances. The mountain monasteries of Fukui Prefecture are frequently snowbound from November through March. I visited the region once, in 1968, for reasons I will not detail here.

---

### Letter Three

*Received September 1953. Postmarked Fukui Prefecture. Paper: thinner than previous letters, with a smoother finish. Ink: standard density, well-ground.*

---

There is an exercise in the Yagyū tradition—you will know it, as your lineage passes through Yagyū Munenori's school—in which the student is instructed to stand before a mirror and hold his stance until he can see it as his opponent would see it. The purpose, according to the teaching scrolls, is the cultivation of objective self-perception. The student learns to identify his own vulnerabilities by adopting the enemy's gaze.

I practiced this exercise for eleven years before competing in Kyoto. I stood before a mirror each morning for the duration of one stick of incense—approximately forty-five minutes—examining my posture, my grip, the angle of my leading foot, the distribution of my weight. I believed I was learning to see myself clearly.

I was wrong.

The mirror exercise does not teach self-perception. It teaches the swordsman to see what *anyone* could see—the gross errors, the visible misalignments, the failures large enough to be captured in reflected light. What it cannot teach is the perception of what is invisible to the practitioner himself, the flaw so deeply integrated into his movement that it has become indistinguishable from his technique, the opening that exists not in the body's architecture but in the space between intention and execution, visible only to the opponent who has achieved correct distance and remained there long enough for the pattern to declare itself.

The mirror shows you your body. Only the opponent shows you your self.

---

**Editor's annotation:** Hideo's description of the Yagyū mirror exercise is accurate, though the tradition from which I received it specifies one incense stick of the shorter variety, approximately twenty-five minutes. This discrepancy may reflect regional variation in the transmission of the form, or a difference in the incense.

I note that this letter contains no drawing.

---

### Letter Four

*Received November 1953. Postmarked Fukui Prefecture. Paper: same stock as Letter Three.*

---

I have been assigned to the kitchen. The abbot believes that repetitive manual labor disciplines the mind. I suspect he believes nothing of the kind and simply needs someone to prepare the radishes.

There is, however, something in the cutting. Not in the technique—I am an indifferent cook and the monks have learned not to expect elegance—but in the moment before the blade enters the vegetable, when the radish sits on the board and my hand positions the knife and there is a pause, briefer than thought, in which the cut exists as pure possibility. In that pause I sometimes see the whole radish—not its surface but its structure, the density of the flesh, the places where it will yield and the places where it will resist, the way the halves will fall.

This is not swordsmanship. I am aware of the absurdity. But the seeing is the same.

*A small ink study of a radish, executed with considerable care. The leaves are rendered in three brushstrokes. The root trails off into a wash that bleeds to the edge of the paper.*

---

**Editor's annotation:** This letter marks the first appearance of what will become a recurring formal pattern in the correspondence: an abstract philosophical inquiry followed by a concrete domestic observation that reframes the abstraction in sensory terms. Whether Hideo is conscious of this structure as a rhetorical strategy or whether it reflects the natural movement of his thought, I cannot determine.

The radish drawing is technically accomplished.

---

### Letter Five

*Received March 1954. Postmarked Fukui Prefecture.*

---

You have not written. I did not expect you to. But I observe that you have not returned the letters either, which tells me your address has not changed, which tells me you have read them, which tells me you have made a decision to continue receiving what you will not answer. This is itself an answer. I accept its terms.

---

**Editor's annotation:** The letter contains no other text. Its brevity is, I believe, calculated.

I had considered not including it.

---

### Letter Six

*Received March 1954. Postmarked Fukui Prefecture. Arrived the same week as Letter Five, possibly posted the same day.*

---

Musashi, in the Fire Book, describes five guards, five stances from which all combat proceeds. He says—and here the commentators agree, which should make us suspicious—that a swordsman must be fluent in all five, moving between them as the situation demands, holding none as permanent.

What he does not say, because it would undermine the system he is constructing, is that every swordsman has a home. A stance to which his body returns when the mind is not watching. A posture that is not chosen but *inhabited*, as natural and as invisible as the way a man holds his shoulders when he believes he is alone.

The home stance is not a technique. It is a self-portrait.

And because it is unchosen, because it exists below the level of instruction, it is the one element of a swordsman's art that training cannot fully address. You can learn to flow between the five guards. You can learn to adopt and release each one with fluency and speed. But in the space between the release of one guard and the adoption of the next—in the transition, which lasts less than a heartbeat—the body passes through its home.
